source: Georg, Stefan. 2007. A Descriptive Grammar of Ket (Yenisei-Ostyak), Part 1: Introduction, Phonology, Morphology. Global Oriental.
claim: Chapter 3 covers tone/prosody, vowels and segmental allophony, consonants and segmental allophony, and phonotactics; Georg explicitly notes that tonal structure strongly conditions segmental allophony.
lect_scope: Ket; dialect distinctions marked in source (SK/CK/NK)
time_scope: modern fieldwork plus earlier Ketological sources where identified

claim: Every Ket monosyllabic stem in isolation bears one of four contrastive suprasegmental entities; Georg argues that contour and phonation, rather than absolute or relative pitch height alone, are their relevant phonetic basis.
Georg transcribes Werner's tone 1 with a macron on the nucleus, tone 2 with a following glottal stop, tone 3 by vowel doubling, and tone 4 with grave accent.

Earlier descriptions often overlooked, ignored, or denied Ket tone; Georg credits Heinrich Werner with its discovery and follows later tone/prosody work while retaining explicit analytical caution about phonetic heterogeneity of the units.
Disyllabic words show two tone-related contours that earlier literature often labels fifth and sixth tones; Georg characterizes them as more accent-like than the four monosyllabic tonemes.

For longer phonological words, the default tendency is for the first two syllables to receive one of the two disyllabic contours while later syllables remain toneless; Georg stresses that longer-chain prosody has not been intensively studied and some distinctions are difficult to verify in present-day fieldwork without experiments.
Vowel Insertion Rule 4 inserts /i/ between two initial consonants of the phonological word in finite verbs, after the P8 marker, repairing an initial cluster.

Georg's core vowel inventory consists of seven phonemes /i ɨ u e ə o a/; open/closed mid-vowel qualities and [ø, œ]-type realizations are treated as predictable or marginal rather than added to the core transcription.

Vowel quantity and, for mid vowels, openness are conditioned by toneme: e.g. /i/ and /ɨ/ are short with tones 2/4, half-long with tone 1, and long/geminated with tone 3; /e/ and /o/ are usually open but have closed half-long realizations with tone 1.
Georg recognizes a compact consonant inventory /b t d k q s h l j m n ŋ/ distributed across labial, alveolar/lateral/palatal, velar, uvular and laryngeal places.

Unlike earlier descriptions and the official orthography, Georg does not recognize /p/ as a regular phoneme: most [p] is analyzed as devoiced /b/ word-finally or adjacent to voiceless consonants, and remaining initial [p] is largely loanword, onomatopoeic, or archaic/unclear; he reports no /p/~/b/ minimal pair.

Georg follows Vajda in rejecting a phonemic plain-versus-palatalized coronal contrast found in earlier treatments; many alleged palatalized/plain pairs vary, robust minimal pairs are lacking, and Russian-speaking researchers may have perceptually overinterpreted 'slurred' coronals as Russian-like palatalization.

Velar and uvular fricative phones are analyzed as intervocalic variants of /k/ and /q/ rather than independent phonemes; apparently final examples are linked historically to earlier intervocalic environments in Northern Ket comparanda.

Initial consonant clusters are generally avoided and arise only in restricted morphosyntactic contexts; speakers may avoid possessive-clitic clusters by using a genitive construction, and P8 markers may delete under morphotactic rules to prevent clusters.

Syllable-final consonant clusters are rare, but productive morphology creates them: nominalizer -s combines with root-final consonants, plural suffixes can create final clusters, and nominalization can even yield final CCC clusters when a continuant is present.
Only /b k d n l ŋ s q/ occur in grammatical morphemes; /q/ is restricted there to the causative marker -q-.
Uvular /q/ is unattested word-finally after high vowels /ɨ i u/ and such combinations are exceptionally rare elsewhere, often arising through assimilation.

Some noun plurals are marked by a change in inherent tone without segmental suffixation; both monosyllabic and disyllabic stems participate, and a further class combines tone change with vowel ablaut.

Many stop-final nouns form contractive plurals by adding a plural suffix while deleting the final consonant; the preceding vowel usually lengthens and the resulting plural commonly receives tone 3 (more rarely tone 1).
